items.question: A machine is bought for ₹2,00,000 and depreciated at 10% p.a. on the Written Down Value method. What is its book value at the end of the 3rd year?
items.explanation: Under WDV, each year's depreciation is 10% of the opening book value, so the charge falls every year. Three years of 10% reduction gives ₹2,00,000 × 0.9³ = ₹1,45,800.

why_not.A: Straight-line: 10% of cost (₹20,000) charged every year.
why_not.C: This is the value after 2 years, not 3.
why_not.D: This is the value after 4 years.

items.exam_tip: Shortcut: book value after n years = Cost × (1 − rate)ⁿ.

items.question: The Cash Book shows a debit balance of ₹25,000. Cheques of ₹6,000 issued to suppliers are not yet presented, and cheques of ₹4,000 deposited are not yet credited by the bank. What is the balance as per the Pass Book?
items.explanation: Cheques issued but not presented have not left the bank account yet, so the Pass Book is higher: add them. Cheques deposited but not credited have not reached the bank account yet: deduct them.

why_not.A: Signs reversed: issued cheques deducted, deposits added.

items.exam_tip: Ask one question: has the bank recorded it yet? Not paid out by the bank means a higher Pass Book balance; not received by the bank means lower.

items.question: Annual requirement of a material is 20,000 units. Ordering cost is ₹100 per order and carrying cost is ₹4 per unit per year. What is the Economic Order Quantity?
items.explanation: EOQ = √(2AO ÷ C). With A = 20,000 units, O = ₹100 and C = ₹4, EOQ = √10,00,000 = 1,000 units.

why_not.A: The 2 in the formula is missing.
why_not.D: That is average inventory (EOQ ÷ 2), not the order size.

items.exam_tip: At EOQ, total ordering cost equals total carrying cost (₹2,000 each here). Use it to check your answer.

items.question: Standard time for a job is 10 hours. A worker finishes it in 8 hours. His rate is ₹50 per hour. What are his earnings for the job under the Halsey Premium Plan (50%)?
items.explanation: Halsey pays time wages plus a bonus of 50% of the time saved at the hourly rate. Time saved is 2 hours, so the bonus is 50% × 2 × ₹50 = ₹50.

why_not.B: Time wages only, bonus left out.
why_not.D: Pays the full standard time, i.e. 100% of time saved.

items.exam_tip: Halsey shares a fixed 50% of time saved; Rowan uses time saved ÷ time allowed. Revise them together.

items.topic: Ind AS 10: Events after the reporting period
items.question: Reporting date is 31 March 2026 and the financial statements are approved on 15 May 2026. On 20 April 2026, a customer owing ₹8 lakh at year-end is declared insolvent; its financial trouble already existed at 31 March. How is this treated under Ind AS 10?
options: Non-adjusting event: disclose in the notes only
Adjusting event: recognise the loss on the receivable in FY 2025-26
Ignore it, as it happened after the reporting date
Recognise the loss in FY 2026-27, when the insolvency occurred
items.explanation: Insolvency of a customer after the reporting date usually confirms the receivable was already impaired at that date. It gives evidence about a condition that existed at 31 March, so it is an adjusting event.

why_not.A: Non-adjusting events reflect conditions that arose after year-end, e.g. a later fall in the value of investments.
why_not.C: Ind AS 10 covers events up to the approval date; they cannot be ignored.
why_not.D: The loss existed at 31 March; deferring it overstates FY 2025-26 assets.

items.exam_tip: One test decides it: did the condition exist on the reporting date? Yes, adjust. No, disclose if material.

items.question: The risk-free rate is 6%, the expected market return is 14% and a share's beta is 1.25. What is the required rate of return on the share as per CAPM?
items.explanation: CAPM: Ke = Rf + β (Rm − Rf). The market risk premium is 8%; beta scales it to 10%; adding the risk-free rate gives 16%.

why_not.A: Beta multiplied by Rm (1.25 × 14%), not by the premium.
why_not.B: Used 6% as the premium instead of 8%.

items.exam_tip: Beta multiplies the premium (Rm − Rf), never Rm itself.
